item.title: When There’s No One Else to Blame
item.description:
Resilience

When There’s No One Else to Blame

What Mongolia’s brutal winter taught me about owning our choices.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Honest self-reflection is more useful than making excuses or punishing yourself for getting things wrong.
  • Ignoring a mistake could turn a manageable problem into a dangerous one.
  • You cannot control everything that happens, but you can take responsibility for how you respond.
  • Thinking ahead about obstacles can help you make better decisions when circumstances change.
Weather Deteriorates, Outlook Bleak
Source: Sean Burch / Used with permission

I've learned a certain kind of accountability in the mountains. It’s not self-blame or just admitting you made a mistake. It’s the willingness to face conditions as they are, own what's yours, and make the next decision before life makes it for you.

In Mongolia, accountability hit home more profoundly than it ever had before.

After nearly two years of planning, I led a Mongolian logistics team into the Altai in winter to support my attempt at a series of solo first ascents. I eventually set a world record for the most first ascents in the country’s history.

But the number of summits is not what stays with me.

I remember the cold.

Temperatures dropped below -30°F. There were avalanches, snowstorms, and blinding winds that knocked me off my feet. I developed hypothermia and suffered frostbite. Some of my fingertips turned black, and the extreme cold left my skin cracked and raw. At one point, I broke through the ice into a freezing river. By the time I freed my boots and snowshoes, it was no longer about discomfort, but rather a race against time.

In those moments, the responsibility was mine. I had conceived the expedition, secured the sponsors, organized the base-camp team and logistics, and chosen to push the challenge further by climbing in winter. My team provided operational support from base camp. The decisions on the mountain were mine to make.

When the weather allowed, the days I spent climbing were filled with self-interrogation: Was I dressed appropriately? Was I reading the terrain correctly? Had I pushed myself too far? I knew no one was coming to save me if I made a mistake.

Experience in the mountains had taught me that debating about a problem, the terrain, or the weather wouldn’t change anything. I had to assess the situation, acknowledge what was going wrong, recognize my own mistakes, and make decisions based on reality, rather than the plan I’d committed to. If I was getting too cold, slowing down, or facing worsening conditions, I had to factor that into my choices. In mountaineering, refusing to acknowledge a problem can cost you your life. Continuing simply because I’d committed to a plan wouldn’t have been courageous. It would have been reckless.

I have since come to believe there’s a question you must ask yourself in every difficult situation, whether at work, at home, in a relationship, or in a predicament you happen to be in: “What part of this is mine?”

article continues after advertisement

I think self-criticism is easily confused with self-accountability. Beating yourself up after something goes wrong, whether it’s your fault or not, doesn't necessarily make you better at handling what comes next.

Accountability begins before the crisis. It means recognizing the signals you can't afford to ignore, preparing for what you can, and accepting your part when things don't go as planned. You may not be responsible for the problem, but you're still responsible for your next move.

That’s why I keep returning to expeditions and challenges in nature. The mountains don’t let you hide behind good intentions, blame, or a plan that no longer fits the conditions. They force you to confront reality, identify what’s yours to own, and act before hesitation becomes a greater threat than the original problem.

Life is hardly a clean slate. Relationships, careers, finances, health, and loss do not offer the simple choices of routes on a map. But the fundamental question remains: What part of this is mine? The answer begins with seeing a situation for what it is, recognizing where you have influence, and taking action where it matters.

Mongolia taught me that accountability does not make hard circumstances disappear. It does something more useful: It keeps you engaged with the part of your life that is still yours to lead.

item.title: 5 Questions to Assess Your Most Unusual Strengths
item.description:
Career

5 Questions to Assess Your Most Unusual Strengths

How to identify strengths you didn't know you had.

Posted October 18, 2026

Source: AI generated image

Jenny, a manager at a large company in Boston, has an idea she wants implemented. She knows her proposal would get immediately shot down if she pitched it out of the blue.

However, Jenny’s unusual strength is that she is willing to spend months figuring out how to get a decision made.

She uses that time to figure out who influences whom, understand individual priorities, and provide help to those she is going to ask to support her idea later.

Most people would balk at that type of lengthy process. They don’t care enough or don’t have the social skills. Jenny quite enjoys it and will happily spend six months or more playing a long game.

Others in Jenny’s organization could do what she does, but they’re not willing to go through it.

Our Strengths Are Often What We’re Willing to Do, Not Just What We’re Capable Of

In my previous writing, I introduced this idea that your strengths are things you’re willing to do that 95% of people aren’t.

Examples:

  • People who are happy to fish, not necessarily catch. They’re okay with intermittent reward, or even attracted to that.
  • Those who are willing to exist with uncertainty for a long time, who can delay making a decision, versus the person who likes to close open questions quickly and move on. For instance, the athlete who’s willing to travel to a race nursing an injury, and not know whether they’re actually going to be able to compete.
  • The person who builds their own tool because they’re not content to put up with the flawed tool most other people in the same role use daily and tolerate as “good enough.”
  • The person who is much more willing to deal with bureaucracy than someone else. The colleague who will take on projects that require submitting docs to four different agencies or who is willing to sit on committees.
  • The person who is willing to learn by “mashing buttons” or asking lots of newbie questions.
  • The person who doesn’t mind working with colleagues others avoid, like the company narcissist, or with people whose values they don’t share.

The 5-Question Framework I Use Now

Since I first wrote about the concept of your strengths being what 95% of other people aren’t willing to do, I've fleshed out the procedure I recommend.

Now I suggest people ask themselves a series of 5 questions.

Start by asking yourself, “What am I willing to do that 50% of people aren’t?” Then ask yourself the same question four more times, raising the percentage to 70%, 90%, 95%, and finally 99%.

article continues after advertisement

At the first 50% level, your strengths are likely to be things you share with lots of other people in your field, like attention to detail or particular social skills.

Your answers will get more interesting when you get up to the higher percentages. The 95% level is where people see ways they’re different from other people in their field, and qualities that can be a positive in one context but perhaps negative in another.

For example, if you’re extremely intolerant of repetition or want to do literally everything in your own bespoke way, those highly unusual qualities are likely to be a source of differentiation and breakthroughs, but also some frustration and wasted time.

Push Yourself Beyond Stereotypical Answers

At first glance, it can seem like unusual strengths boil down to just a few contrasts, or even clichés, like:

  • the cautious person vs. the risk-taker
  • the lone wolf marching to the beat of their own drum vs. the person who is very socially strategic with an extensive network

When you work through the 5-question framework for yourself, try to get away from these types of answers.

Imagine a woman in commercial real estate trying to make a complicated deal work. For her, obstacles are like a red rag to a bull. She almost enjoys having another obstacle to work around. She’s already thinking of three alternative routes. She gets amped up when someone says no, or when a condition changes yet again, requiring another hurdle to be jumped. That kind of unusual strength escapes clichés associated with atypical high performers.

Why 5 Questions

You might be wondering what the point of this being a series of 5 questions is. It’s for contrast. It also helps lubricate your thinking and not miss things. For example, staggering the questions might help you think of an offshoot of a more common strength as one of your later answers.

article continues after advertisement

Let yourself sit with these questions for awhile. Don't be concerned if answers don't immediately come to mind. Even after a few months of noticing your behavior through this perspective, you might identify strengths you originally overlooked.

item.title: Why My Spirit Needs My Daily Photos
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Why My Spirit Needs My Daily Photos

Personal Perspective: I stop, breathe, give thanks, or just clear my mental air.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Instead of "Morning walk," I now caption my daily Facebook photos "Morning prayer."
  • At first, I worried I would look like a religious nut.
  • I'm not an overtly prayerful person, but I was comfortable with this gentle reminder.

I have always been a walker and a watcher. I study the details of neighborhood houses and in the nearby pond, and on the evergreens near our mountain cabin. Walks keep me energized and sane. Without them, my system turns to ick. For years, I have taken my Facebook friends with me and posted photos of my strolls; I captioned them “morning walk.” A few months ago, I changed that to “morning prayer.”

The idea came to me, as many ideas do, from lunch with a friend. She was distraught about the state of our country and felt her acts of resistance were futile. I think all I have left is prayer, she said. I told her I’d been feeling the same thing.

I thought about this a bit and decided to turn my photos into prayers and post them.

I was uncomfortable doing this at first, worrying that I would come off as some sort of religious nut. Liberals too often hide their spirituality out of a sense of moral politeness. Yet most of my like-minded friends are regular churchgoers, and our church community is an essential part of our lives.

I am not an overtly prayerful person, although I’ve always prayed, one way or another. I attended Catholic schools from first grade through high school. As a kid, I went to church most Sundays and many weekdays, carrying my little white leather prayer book until I became way too cool for it. Usually, I daydreamed during Mass, but I always followed the prayers. I found them meditative.

I’m totally unqualified to have any sort of theological discussion, despite all that education, but I have benefitted from the wisdom of the many holy women I am fortunate to call friends. They have taught me that prayer can be formal but doesn’t need to be. It can be an essential part of a religious service, but it also exists outside of religion. Maybe that’s where it lives most strongly for me.

My morning Facebook prayers initially were of the sunrise from our balcony, because it was too cold to go for much of a walk, and nature was monochromatic. Plus, the sunrise felt like an act of God. Then I added shots of the sunset or the moon as an evening prayer. As spring came, the shots turned into irises and roses, ponds, and budding trees. Sometimes I add an afternoon prayer if I have spillover beauty. Now, they sparkle in autumn's gold.

The photos are a chance for me to stop, breathe, give gratitude, ask for help, express sorrow, or do whatever else my spirit needs. My friends can join me or scroll right on. I’m not telling them to pray; I’m just sharing what makes me prayerful.

Religion does not always mean goodness and virtue. Sadly, throughout history, it’s often meant the opposite. But anyone can pray. And my daily photos of nature’s beauty give me a reason to at least inhale and give thanks.

article continues after advertisement

It’s much better than inhaling the venom that too often fills my screen.

Recently a former student messaged me in thanks for a photo of a flower I had just posted as a prayer. It reminded her of her mother, who had died a couple years ago. She sent the note in the evening, and we had a sweet virtual conversation, right before I headed to bed.

“I’m so glad we reconnected,” she said.

“Me too,” I answered.

To me, that was an answer to a prayer. I fell asleep that night with a memory of a beloved mother, a peony, and a treasured student. And when I woke up the next morning and wanted to be lazy, I put on my clothes instead and went to the park, phone in hand, looking for prayers.

item.title: Love and Its Problems
item.description:
Relationships

Love and Its Problems

How to avoid love problems.

Posted October 18, 2026

What is love? There are various types of love. You can love a piece of music, a food, your pet dog, a favorite city, or working out in the gym. However the emotion of interpersonal love consists of an intense feeling of deep affection, intense liking, and strong preference for another person, accompanied by caring and commitment. It also involves enjoying being with the individual, concern for their well-being, and missing them when the two of you are apart.

Despite what many psychologists may tell you, when you feel emotionally disturbed within the context of a love relationship, it's not your childhood upbringing or relationship with your parents that determine your current emotional disturbance. These may be factors and influences, along with your life experiences and genetic predispositions, but rather it's your current disturbed thinking about these experiences that cause your love problems. Love itself is not the trouble. The difficulty begins when you escalate your love preferences into demands. Demands consist of absolutistic, rigid, universal, dogmatic, unconditional, necessities.

Some of the most common demands individuals are likely to harbor in a love relationship are:

  • I absolutely must be loved by the person I love.
  • I need my partner's approval otherwise this means I am an unlovable individual.
  • Since no one loves me this proves I'm unlovable.
  • I can't stand living without a love partner.
  • It's awful, terrible, horrible, and the end of my world not to have love in my life.

Ironically, demanding to be loved tends to push people away and, consequently, frequently leads to less love. It may feel needy, suffocating, or desperate to a partner.

Suppose you were criticized by your partner and you're feeling hurt. The good news is that it's your belief about the criticism, not the criticism itself, that causes your hurt feelings. And you can change your thinking to get over your hurt feelings.

  • A. Activating Event: I was rejected by the person I love.
  • B. Irrational Belief: I absolutely need his or her approval.
  • C. Undesirable Emotional Consequences: Hurt and depressed.
  • D. Questioning or Debating the Irrational Belief: What is the evidence I absolutely need his or her approval?
  • E. Effective New Thinking or the Answer to the Question: There is no evidence that supports my conviction that it's a dire necessity I have his or her approval. Although I strongly prefer the person I love, love me, I do not absolutely have to be loved by him or anyone else. Although I distinctly do not like it when he criticizes or disapproves of me, I definitely can rationally stand what I do not like. His rejection of my love is unfortunate but hardly the end of the world or the end of my life. I can unconditionally accept myself with his rejection as the imperfect fallible human I am.
  • F. New Feeling Resulting From E: Great disappointment, intense regret, extreme dissatisfaction, strong frustration, rather than hurt and depression.

item.title: Can We Choose Confidence?
item.description:
Confidence

Can We Choose Confidence?

Jake Bauers, the Milwaukee Brewers, and the physiology of confidence and belief.

Posted October 18, 2026

The Milwaukee Brewers just swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, and Jake Bauers was named MVP. After Game 4, he said, “I chose to be confident. I chose to believe in myself.” A game earlier, he had reflected, “I stopped caring about results. I started caring about competing.”

When Bauers joined FOX’s postgame panel—Alex Rodriguez, David Ortiz, Derek Jeter, and host Kevin Burkhardt—they discussed his, and the Brewers’, confidence and belief. They described that confidence as something you could feel in the clubhouse or see in the dugout. Despite being swept by the Dodgers the year before, the Brewers gave the impression that they expected to win this series all along.

And then the commentators went searching for explanations.

We often describe confidence intuitively as a feeling, as a presence we recognize in ourselves and others. Yet we somehow forget this when we describe how we find it or come to feel it. We put so much emphasis on mindset. On intention. On making a choice or decision. On remembering who we are and what we’ve done before. Bauers’ own words echo that emphasis. And to be fair, these approaches can all be helpful. As can accepting that we will sometimes strike out, staying with the process, and letting go of the outcome. But if deciding to remain in the moment and be confident were all it took, wouldn’t we all do it?

Haven’t we all been told at some point, “Just relax. Let it come to you. Trust yourself. Remember what you’re capable of. Go out there and have fun”?

I imagine Shohei Ohtani, the Dodgers’ best player and arguably the greatest player in baseball, told himself, and heard from his coaching staff, much the same. Yet, while dealing with knee and biceps injuries, he hit only .192 in the postseason, going 5-for-26 with 10 strikeouts. Knowing what he is capable of cannot, by itself, make such high performance available on demand, especially when injured. Yet we like to think we can just focus more and try harder, and our body will respond accordingly.

In contrast, consider what Bauers was doing at the plate. In consecutive games, he worked a 12-pitch walk against Yoshinobu Yamamoto and hit a home run on the 11th pitch against Blake Snell. David Ortiz, the Hall of Famer and three-time World Series champion, described those two at-bats as among the most impressive he had ever seen.

Making contact with a baseball roughly 2.9 inches across traveling at 100 mph takes extraordinary timing and precision: Picking up information from the pitcher’s delivery. Mapping the ball’s flight. Anticipating speed and path of motion. Adjusting to different pitches while remaining ready for the one you want to hit. This depends on coordinated eye, head, and body movements, including picking up on the spin of the ball and looking ahead toward the ball’s anticipated path. And all of this happens within a fraction of a second.

Much of what allows a hitter to do all of this in the blink of an eye unfolds without consciously directing each movement. In fact, in research using simulated batting, asking expert hitters to attend closely to their swing mechanics increased errors and movement variability. A conscious intention can guide an approach. But executing that approach in real time involves capacities that extend beyond what we can consciously coordinate in the moment.

Stephen W. Porges’ more recent framework of physiological state and accessibility provides another way to understand what we may be watching. Within this framework, physiological state organizes which capacities are available for recruitment and expression. Having developed a capacity, such as hitting a major-league fastball, and being able to access that capacity under pressure in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series are different parts of the performance equation.

article continues after advertisement

From this perspective, we can think of physiology as giving us “permission” for what’s possible and probable. Our skills, knowledge, intentions, and experience may still be there, while our access to them changes as our physiology changes. Intending to stay relaxed, confident, and present, and being able to see, anticipate, and respond with precision are connected. But the intention alone does not account for everything that makes hitting a baseball possible.

Bauers describes a change in how he approaches the game. I’m interested in the physiology of that change. How his new approach and his physiological responses are linked. Who and what has helped make that possible for him now, within this team, within his family, within this culture, and within some of the biggest moments of his career?

Bauers offered one part of that story: “We play for each other.” He described teammates responding to mistakes by looking for ways to help one another. Those relationships and repeated experiences can shape physiological responses beneath the words. Trusted relationships can help make acceptance something a player can truly feel and authentically act on.

What becomes possible when falling short does not leave us feeling alone? When we have less to prove about ourselves with every outcome? When the people around us help us stay connected to the game we love, to one another, to why we are doing this, and to what we are capable of doing, whether we win or lose?

His intentions may be part of that change. They may help shape his physiological responses, just as those responses shape his access to confidence and belief. But when Bauers describes choosing “to be confident” or deciding to “stop caring about results,” those words alone don't make it happen. Those intentions become something he can actually feel and act on to the degree that his physiological state makes them accessible under pressure. Otherwise, they’re just words we tell ourselves and the media.

We cannot define every process that makes a physiological shift possible. We also cannot determine a player’s physiological state from the results alone. A physiological state that supports access to their full range of capacities does not guarantee a home run when the game is on the line, and we may never know all the factors shaping Bauers' physiological responses.

article continues after advertisement

But can we start to look beneath words and intentions a bit more? Can we recognize and respect the role physiology plays, and learn to appreciate it, accept it, and come alongside it?

When we tell ourselves to relax, trust the process, or go out there and have fun, can we also become curious about who and what would help our physiology organize in a way that makes those experiences accessible?

Between our potential and our performance under pressure is our physiological state. That’s why accepting whatever shows up can be helpful. That’s why trusting our teammates can strengthen our belief in ourselves. That’s why it matters to know in our minds, and feel in our bodies, that we are valued and belong, win or lose.

Call it confidence. Call it belief. Call it team chemistry. Call it a new approach. But recognize the physiological state beneath it.

Bauers and the Brewers seemed to have found a way to feel safe enough to play within the pressure.
